turn2.differences: The author's three conditions (c1 name, c2 start date, c3 Urgent issue assigned to Priya Nair) match my step-1 conditions closely. The author omits an explicit year for the start date and doesn't call out the multi-team \"Cycle 14\" naming collision, but neither omission changes the outcome: only one record (c-web-14) satisfies all three conditions once the data is checked. The action (moving the end date to Oct 20) is correctly left out of the filtering conditions since it's the operation to perform, not a selection criterion.

ambiguity_effects.explain: All cycle data in the workspace is dated 2026, and today's date (2026-09-26) makes 2026-09-29 the only sensible reading of an imminent cycle start. No other year's data exists to create real uncertainty, so this resolves cleanly and doesn't change which cycle matches.

ambiguity_effects.explain: The dataset only exposes a single current cycleId per issue, with no history of past cycle reassignment, so there is no alternate 'historical' reading to apply here -- both readings collapse to the same check against cycleId.

Three different teams (Web, Growth, Mobile) each have a cycle literally named "Cycle 14", so the name alone is not unique. But the combination of the start-date condition (c2) and the issue condition (c3) narrows this to exactly one record, c-web-14, so the team-scope ambiguity is fully resolved by the rest of the sentence and does not leave a careful reader unsure about the final answer.

turn2.naturalness_note: The request reads like a plausible real-world instruction from someone juggling cycles across multiple teams in the same org, where cycle numbers and start dates can coincide -- the extra qualifiers (start date, an Urgent issue assigned to a specific person) are exactly the kind of detail a real user would add to disambiguate when they know cycle names repeat across teams. Nothing in the phrasing feels artificial or test-specific.
